courseTitle: NativeScript + Angular: Build Native iOS, Android & Web Apps

cues.en: In the previous course modules, we spent a lot of work on working on the UI and working on the look
of the app, and in the last course section, we, of course had a look at how we can fetch user input
and work with forums in our native app.
In this module, we'll have a look at managing our state and therefore adding some logic to our application.
And therefore we need to know what exactly application state is.
Of course.
Now, consider this app here, which is not the app we're building, but consider an app where we have
a home component, a product list component and a new product component where we can maybe create a
new product that is then listed in our shop.
We might be building here now in ANGULAR.
We then use services to manage the state.
And as always, when we talk about angular services are a concept you should be familiar with.
Definitely dive into the refresher or some dedicated angular resources if you want to learn more about
them.
A service could be used for fetching a product and for storing a new product so services can act as
middlemen between your different pages and the application, different components which are not directly
in a parent child relationship.
This is the so-called application state, which is typically lost when the app refreshes in a browser
or on a mobile app.
If the app restarts or was idle for a longer time and therefore what we also typically do is we store
data on a backend on a server, so we store and fetch data there and that is then persistance state.
So a state can mean a couple of different things.
But in this module we'll work on the application state and later in a later course section will then
work on storing that state on a server.
Now, what will do in this module?
Data for us will work with services and with models that reflect our data and will make sure that in
our Challenge app we can actually create and replace challenges, that we also can mark individual days
as completed or failed, and that all of that gets reflected in our user interface.
And then later sections will then work on storing that on a server or fetching it from there and on
user authentication.
